script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Today we'll look at the water cycle, one of the most important processes on Earth.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: It begins with evaporation. The sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, turning it into vapour.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: This warm, moist air rises into the atmosphere and slowly cools down.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: As it cools, condensation occurs. The vapour turns into tiny water droplets, forming clouds.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: When these droplets become too heavy, precipitation follows. Rain or snow falls back to the ground.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Some of this water flows into rivers and returns to the sea. Some soaks into the soil.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Water underground is called groundwater. It can stay there for thousands of years.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Plants also play a role. Through transpiration, they release water vapour from their leaves.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Interestingly, about ninety-seven percent of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Only three percent is fresh water, and most of that is frozen in glaciers.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: So the water we drink today may once have fallen as rain on the dinosaurs.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Next week, we'll examine how climate change is affecting this cycle.

title: Lecture: The Industrial Revolution
titleVi: Bài giảng: Cách mạng công nghiệp

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late eighteenth century.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Before this period, most goods were made by hand in small workshops.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: The invention of the steam engine changed everything. Factories could now run day and night.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: James Watt improved the steam engine in seventeen seventy-six, making it far more efficient.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Textile mills were among the first factories. They produced cloth much faster than hand weavers.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: As a result, thousands of people moved from the countryside to the cities to find work.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: This rapid growth created serious problems: overcrowded housing and dangerous working conditions.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Children as young as six worked twelve-hour days in the mills.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: However, the revolution also brought progress. Railways connected distant towns for the first time.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: By eighteen fifty, Britain produced more coal and iron than the rest of the world combined.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: The changes spread to Europe and America in the nineteenth century.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: In short, this period transformed human society more than any event before it.

title: Talk: Recycling and Waste Management
titleVi: Thuyết trình: Tái chế và quản lý rác thải

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Thank you all for coming to today's talk on recycling.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Every year, the average person throws away about five hundred kilograms of rubbish.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Nearly half of this could be recycled, but most of it ends up in landfill.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Landfill sites are filling up fast, and they produce harmful gases.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: The good news is that recycling one aluminium can saves enough energy to run a TV for three hours.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Glass is another success story. It can be recycled again and again without losing quality.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: However, not everything can go in the recycling bin. Plastic bags often cause problems at recycling plants.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Food waste is a separate issue. In this city, we collect it every Tuesday in the green bins.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Composting food waste creates rich soil for parks and gardens.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Remember the three Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle. Reducing waste is the most important step.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: If everyone recycled just ten percent more, we would save millions of tonnes of waste each year.

script.speaker: Officer
script.textEn: Thank you. I'll now take your questions.

title: Lecture: The Human Brain
titleVi: Bài giảng: Bộ não con người

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: The human brain weighs about one point four kilograms, yet it controls everything we do.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: It contains roughly eighty-six billion nerve cells, called neurons.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: These neurons communicate through tiny electrical signals.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: The largest part of the brain is the cerebrum, which handles thinking and memory.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: The cerebellum, at the back, controls balance and movement.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Interestingly, the brain itself feels no pain. It has no pain receptors.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Your brain uses about twenty percent of the body's total energy.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Sleep is essential for the brain. During sleep, it organises memories from the day.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Contrary to popular belief, we use far more than ten percent of our brains.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Brain scans show that almost all areas are active, even during simple tasks.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: Finally, the brain never stops changing. Learning creates new connections throughout life.

script.speaker: Professor
script.textEn: That's why it's never too late to learn something new.

title: Lecture: Renewable Energy
titleVi: Bài giảng: Năng lượng tái tạo

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Today we'll discuss renewable energy sources and their growing importance.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Solar power is the fastest-growing energy source in the world.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: The cost of solar panels has fallen by eighty percent in the last ten years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Wind energy is another major player. A single modern turbine can power fifteen hundred homes.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: However, both solar and wind depend on the weather, which makes them unreliable at times.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: This is why energy storage is so important. Batteries store extra power for calm or cloudy days.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Hydropower, from dams and rivers, provides steady electricity in many countries.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Norway, for example, gets almost all its electricity from hydropower.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Geothermal energy uses heat from deep inside the Earth. Iceland is a world leader in this field.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: The main challenge for all renewables is cost, though prices continue to fall.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Experts predict that renewables will provide half the world's electricity by twenty thirty-five.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.textEn: Next lecture, we'll look at nuclear energy and its controversies.
